headline: Quiet Tuesday, then a wetter, windier pattern from Wednesday, with the strongest storm likely Friday bringing wind, rain, mountain snow and high surf.
summary: As of Monday night, tonight and Tuesday are mostly quiet. A weak system may bring a small chance of light showers along the coast, over the Olympics and perhaps in the Northwest Interior. Skies stay cloudy, and Tuesday highs should reach the upper 50s, maybe the low 60s in the Southwest Interior. The weather turns more active Wednesday afternoon, when a front brings widespread rain and high-elevation snow. The heaviest rain, perhaps a half inch, is expected along the coast, over the Olympics and in the North Cascades. The Puget Sound area will likely be sheltered by the Olympics (a rain shadow) and may get only a shower or two. Snow levels of about 5000 to 5500 feet mean a few inches of snow on the higher Olympic and Cascade peaks. Southerly winds pick up Wednesday evening, with gusts of 25 to 35 mph on the coast and up to 25 mph inland, then wind and rain ease by Thursday morning. After a brief lull Thursday, a stronger storm is possible late Thursday into Friday, with gusty winds, lowland rain, heavy snow in the high mountains and high surf on the Pacific coast. The surf brings a risk of beach erosion and danger near beaches and jetties. Forecasters give about a 50% chance of damaging-level gusts, which is not a certainty. A short break is possible Friday night into Saturday, but more systems look likely from late in the weekend into the first half of next week. Timing of those later systems is less certain because computer model runs spread out. No watches or warnings are in effect for land areas. River flooding is not expected in the next seven days, though repeated rain will soak the ground and raise rivers, which could matter for later storms.
changes: Early discussions described a foggy morning with a slight chance of showers tonight. By evening, attention shifted to the midweek and Friday storms. The Friday storm was described as potentially the strongest, and forecasters added that more systems look likely from late in the weekend into early next week.
